alt: Three rising steps: moral condemnation, economic sanctions and, as a last resort, military action using members' own forces. A box notes the weak point: no army of its own and unanimous decisions, so every step depended on willing members.
caption: Collective security depended on members being willing to act.

alt: Bars on a 1920-1940 scale show membership: Britain and France throughout, Italy until 1937, Japan until 1933, Germany from 1926 to 1933, the USSR from 1934 until its expulsion in 1939, and the USA never.
caption: Only Britain and France were members throughout.

alt: A table of four disputes: Vilna (1920) a failure, the Aaland Islands (1920-21) a success, Corfu (1923) a failure, and Bulgaria (1925) a success. The pattern: success with smaller states, failure when a great power was involved.
caption: The League worked for small states, not against great powers.

alt: Four cards: Nansen's refugee work, the Health Organisation, the ILO (whose proposals many members did not adopt) and the Slavery Convention of 1926. A note: lasting, but not the League's main aim.
caption: Lasting achievements, but not in the League's main task of preventing war.

alt: A comparison of Manchuria (1931-33) and Abyssinia (1935-36) by cause, trigger, League action, outcome and wider effect. In Manchuria the Lytton Commission condemned Japan but no sanctions followed; in Abyssinia sanctions excluded oil, Suez stayed open and the Hoare-Laval Pact leaked. Both aggressors kept their gains.
caption: In both crises the League condemned the aggressor and the aggressor kept its gains.

alt: A balance. In Manchuria, US absence mattered: sanctions were pointless while the USA kept trading with Japan. In Abyssinia it did not: Britain and France chose not to ban oil or close Suez. Judgement: the leading members' own interests mattered more.
caption: Abyssinia shows the League failed mainly through its own leading members.
